analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Thank you, gentlemen. The case is submitted. We'll resume at 1 o'clock. Mr. Elman, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Thank you, Your Honor. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, this is a land-use regulatory taking case that comes from the State of California. The California State Courts dismissed appellants' complaint in this case for legal insufficiency. Finding it insufficient to state a claim for relief under the 5th and 14th Amendments of the United States Constitution. And under Title 42, Section 1983 of the United States Code. Now, as a result of that procedural situation, we stand before you asking for a remand of this case to the California courts for trial of issues of fact. And the issues of fact will address the three key elements of a regulatory taking case. And I'd like to frame those issues because I'd like to discuss each of them, or at least aspects of each of them in the argument today, within the framework of our complaint. The first is the question of ripeness. What if we can prove, as we have alleged in the complaint, that what occurred in this case was not simply the denial of a subdivision map, but the imposition of regulations which preclude the County of Yolo and the City of Davis from allowing any use of the property of any kind whatsoever, except uses for agricultural and open space? It is our contention that under the ripeness theory articulated by this Court in the Hamilton Bank case and the other cases which have dealt with that issue, that such a result would be a definitive result, definitively applying the regulations to the property in question, and that those determinations are essentially issues of fact for a trial. Now, assuming that we overcome that hurdle, what if we can prove, as we have alleged in our complaint, that the restrictions applied to the property of McDonald's, Summer & Freitas deprive that property of all of its economic beneficial use and deprive the property owner of their reasonable investment-backed expectations? It is our contention that if we succeed in doing that, that we will have established a taking, a regulatory taking, within the precedents which this Court has articulated, some of them as recently as the Connolly case, which I guess is just about a month old today. And finally, if we prove the restriction as I have described it, and if we approve its impact as we have pleaded it, what is the remedy? And here, as you, I'm sure, are aware, the California Courts have categorically denied that there is any possibility to recover compensation in a regulatory taking context. Indeed, if you will look at footnote 57, at page 27 of our reply brief, we have given you some history on the Gilliland litigation where the California Supreme Court has gone to great lengths to cause a depublication of an opinion of the Court of Appeal that suggested that its position on the issue of compensation might be somewhat different than that which is held by this Court here. What is the significance, counsel, of depublication from the Supreme Court of California to a Court of Appeals? The opinion, when it's depublished under the rules, can no longer be cited as authoritative in California courts. So, for all practical purposes, the opinion ceases to exist for everybody except the litigants who are the subject of the decision. It's a race to the parties. Yes, between the parties, yes. Collateralist stops any other issue that they may raise. And I take it that that position in California courts means that you would not have an opportunity to prove what you say you can prove in this case. Well, yes, that's true, Your Honor. And actually, the Court has decided against us in California. So the California issues, I think, have been resolved. And I think it's Joint Appendix 132 or right thereabouts. Why are you precluded now from proving what you say you can prove at trial? As far as, well, because the California Court has said we failed to state a cause of action. And for what reason? First, because we're seeking compensation. Now, is that an independent ground? Yes, I think it is. Well, is there another independent ground? Well, the Court also said because we failed to plead a taking by the taking standard, which it applies. And you see, I mean, that is an issue which we believe implicates federal constitutional principles. The California Court has from time to time said that a regulation which is excessively burdensome as to a property owner, notwithstanding the fact that it's a legitimate exercise of the police power. Well, what's wrong with this saying on what was before it that you didn't plead a taking? Well, I think... Because they just misunderstood what the law was? I think so, Your Honor. In terms of your well-pleaded complaint? Yes, sir. And if one of the... And if you will... It's a confusing opinion. If you will look at page 129 of the Joint Appendix, you will see where the Court agrees that we have well-pleaded the issue of futility, and yet later on in the opinion, the Joint Appendix 134, I believe, the Court says, nonetheless, having pleaded futility, we should have made another application. I mean, it doesn't really make much sense. Well, didn't the Court of Appeals specifically find that a less intensive development proposal might be approved? The Court of Appeals said that in the second half of its opinion. And aren't we bound by that? I do not think so, Your Honor. Why not? Because I think that we have stated a case for relief under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment, of which this Court is the final arbiter, when we plead in our complaint, bear in mind what occurred here. We plead that any application would be futile. Yes, but the Court of Appeals says not so. Well, the Court of Appeals said not so on a case dispositive pleading motion. I mean, I don't think that if it is possible for a State Court to find against a complaint on a case dispositive pleading motion, relying on the findings of the defendant in the case, the County Board of Supervisors, if you will, you're in a situation where a plaintiff who accuses a local governing body of having violated your constitutional rights can insulate itself from any liability by making a finding that it hasn't done so, which the Court will then rely upon to prevent a trial. See, we were denied a trial in this case on that issue. Essentially, the record was, we plead no use. And the County comes back and says, yeah, you have a use. And the Court of Appeal found their finding conclusive, not even allowing us to go to trial. I submit, and it's our theory here, that if that's what the California courts have decided, it does not meet constitutional standards because it effectively deprives us of a constitutional right. But the observation of the California Supreme Court, or rather the California Court of Appeals, was that if you had asked for a less intensive residential use, and you were asking for some more than four homes to the acre, as I recall, perhaps the zoning board would have gone along. Is that just flatly wrong? It is flatly wrong. But certainly contrary to your allegations in the complaint. It's contrary to the allegations of our, you mean that it was wrong? No, no, that you said it would have been futile, and that's one of the issues that you would want to try out. That's correct. And our complaint frames the issue. We have the burden of proving it, and I submit to you, if we can't prove that, we lose. It's just that simple. But it's not an issue which can be determined conclusively by the other side putting its submittal in and having that submittal found as conclusive. You know, it defended— Well, it sounds like what you're complaining about is that the California courts didn't give you your day in court. They didn't let you have a hearing. Well, in— And that would be some, what, some kind of a due process claim? It isn't a takings claim. Well, Your Honor, what they did is they established— I think it's right. They established—they reached a decision, in effect, which deprived us of our right to pursue our takings claim. They decided in effect that the findings of the defendant, the defendant county of Yolo, were going to be conclusive and prevent us from having a trial. But more importantly than that, it's a forum which absolutely denies what we claim is a constitutionally mandated remedy. We claim that we're entitled to compensation. The California courts say— Well, you're not entitled to compensation unless there's a taking. And it sounds like you're saying we can't prove a taking because they won't let us go to trial. That's correct. And that isn't a question here, then, of taking. It's a question of whether California furnished you due process of law, I guess. Well, Your Honor, I—it is our position that it becomes a question of a taking because we claim that under our complaint that we pleaded the issue of futility and ripeness and the court of appeal agreed and by the standard of what we ought to be entitled to do in order to vindicate our constitutional rights, that that should be enough. It is not enough for the court to then go on and say, well, they pleaded futility, but it wasn't futile because they could have made another application. This court sits in judgment to review what the courts below have done on constitutional issues, and that's essentially our position. I am as puzzled, I must confess, by what the court of appeal did as between those parts of the opinion as you appear to be. I mean, I can't reconcile them. Mr. Elman, may I ask you one question? Yes, sir. Under your view of the case, when did the taking occur? The taking occurred when we were denied our subdivision approval in the process by which that denial occurred. That would be in June of 1977? Well, the findings of fact were actually made in February, I believe, in 77. It became final in June of 77, and that would be about right, yes. And when did you file this complaint? October of 1977. Well, the fourth amended complaint was filed in 1981. I see. And when did you file your case in which you sought mandamus or equitable relief? The mandamus case was originally filed concurrently with the filing of the case seeking damages. Does California procedure provide for those to go forward jointly, or why would they go forward separately? Well, the mandate case is a case which is in the nature of appellate review. It's initiated by a petition, and it's tried on an administrative record. And typically, you file it with a memorandum of points and authorities, and an alternative writ is issued, which directs the administrative body to set aside what it's done subject to review of the administrative record. It's not like a case initiated with a complaint followed by an answer and with discovery. Why wouldn't that case in the normal course of events have gone forward before this one? That's one thing the puzzle is. Well, I can give you some history on the mandate case. At the time this lawsuit was initiated, this Court had not yet decided Penn Central, and there was tremendous uncertainty in the law as it developed. In addition to that, it was our perception that you could not comfortably join a mandate action as part of an action, a normal civil action, which might proceed on the basis of discovery and with an answer and proceed in the ordinary course. As the litigation developed, though, when it became clear that the California courts were only going to allow the remedy of invalidation as a result of the mandate petition, we took the position that that was a constitutionally inadequate remedy. And so that... Well, how could you take that position without finding out first what kind of relief you might have gotten? Well, because the California courts have told us that all you're entitled to in a mandate case is to set aside the decision below when you go back and they reapply a different set of restrictions. But is it not conceivable that in that case you would have gotten precisely what the Court said at the end of its opinion in this case, that you have a right to file an application for a less intensive use? No, sir, and I would like to explain to you why, if I may. And unfortunately, this requires you to get into a little bit, into the quagmire of the California land planning law, but you don't have to decide the issue because it's just a question that can be referred back for trial. California requires that all approvals be found consistent with a valid and internally consistent general plan. Now, the general plan consists of several elements. There's a land use element which designated this property as residential, but there are also development policies. And the development policy, which was applied to us and found controlling in this case, we've set out in pertinent part in footnote 3 on page 3 of our reply brief. And it's a development policy that says that notwithstanding the fact that we've designated this land residential, it cannot be developed until it's annexed to the City of Davis, because we, the county of Yolo, even though we're the planning jurisdiction and even though we have determined with our planners hat on that residential is the most appropriate use of the property, you can't develop or make any use of the property that requires urban service until you take the property into Davis. And Davis came to our hearing, to the hearing on our findings, and said our law controls, our ordinances control, we have this zoned agricultural and open space, and furthermore, Yolo County, you lack the authority to grant any approval. Now, we can prove a trial. This is essentially, as the party whose complaint was dismissed, I suppose I make this in the nature of an offer of proof, but I think it's well within the terms of our pleadings. We can prove a trial that Yolo County, under the authorities I've cited in footnote 4 of our reply brief, lacks the legal authority to grant us the right to do anything. The California Court of Appeal did not recognize that, but if you read the Friends of B Street case or the Save El Toro case or the other cases I've cited, you will see that with the county having applied that development policy to us... That's very difficult, Mr. Ellman. You know, when we have a Court of Appeals opinion in your case that doesn't say that at all, for you to tell us that other California cases say something... We're not authorities on California law. Presumably the judges of the California Court of Appeal are. Well, Your Honor, I understand that, and I appreciate the difficulty, and I think that the area of the law is peculiar to California. There is no question about that. All I am prepared... All we're asking for... We're not asking you to resolve those issues. We are... What I am saying to you is that we have pleaded that, notwithstanding what the Court of Appeals said, that it would be futile for us to make any other application, and that Yolo County could not grant us any approval, and we can prove that at trial, and that we are entitled... Well, then, for you to win, we have to disagree with the California Court of Appeals on an issue of California state law, as I understand you. I don't believe that is true, Justice O'Connor, with all due respect. I think that you need only say that if we can plead, if we can prove what we have pleaded, a very simple, straightforward question, that we have stated a case, a takings case, cognizable under the 5th and 14th Amendment in 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. Now, the... That sounds like an advisory opinion or something in the face of a holding by the California Court to the effect that you can't do that, that you could seek application for a less intensive development with a chance of success. Well, if you... I disagree with that, but obviously... I mean, we... But I would like to suggest one thing to you. If you look at the California Court of Appeal opinion, you will see the last part of the opinion talks about the Civil Rights Act, the 42 U.S.C. Section 1983, and it says that, well, we didn't plead a due process case, so we're not entitled to a remedy. Without... I mean the court... I mean the California Court of Appeal, no disrespect, but I mean that is a proposition so plainly erroneous that it ought to suggest some at least question about the internal integrity of that opinion. I believe... It's our position, and if it isn't sufficient here, then that will be the decision of the court, that we're asking you to remand to the California Trial Court advising that court that if we can prove what we've alleged, that there's no other application available to us, and that we can prove that those restrictions deprived us of all economic beneficial use of our property, then we have met the test of rightness, and we've established a taking. What was your property zoned in the county of Yolo when you made the application? Residential. We were in accordance with all of the applicable zoning and general plan designations. And your submission was in accordance with the setback and minimum lot area? Yes, sir. It complied in all those respects. The only problem was is that it did not comply with this development policy. And the development policy was not to allow any residential building in Yolo County until the part was annexed to the city of Davis? That's correct. And a lot of California counties have somewhat similar policies. Now, the county board of supervisors found a number of deficiencies... Other reasons. Right. But our pleading is, and as I say, we are prepared to prove a trial, that the application complied in all respects with every land use regulation ordinance of the county of Yolo applicable to that property at the time except this development policy. Well, then, what is the California law when you submit your subdivision map, which I presume asks approval for the subdivision, if everything complies with every existing zoning regulation, what discretion does the board of supervisors have? Well, they have the discretion to deny it on several grounds. First, in this case, they applied a development policy to override the land use element, which is fairly common. And that is consistent with California law, I think. Correct. And see, we are not arguing. We pleaded in our complaint a number of aspects where we thought that what they did to us was wrong, to use a generic, imprecise term. But the fact is that I think those are California issues and that we stand here having to admit that what has occurred is a legitimate exercise of the police power as the California court views it. But as I think you, sir, wrote for the court in Kaiser Aetna, the question of whether or not there is a taking is a wholly separate question. And that's the wholly separate question that we're attempting to present here. Mr. Ellman, was this development policy adopted by the county after your client bought the property? Yes, I believe so. I see. And that then, but you don't contend that was the taking, adopting the policy? No, because it wasn't applied. You see, if we had come to this court, if we had filed a case without having made an application and I was standing here trying to tell you that that was going to be applied to override the land use element, you would say, don't tell me that until you've made an application as I read Agins and we have to throw it. Yes, but the Court of Appeals has now told us you can make another application. So I'm not really sure it's all that different if it is the development policy that totally frustrates your use of the property. Well, our problem, and I understand, I understand that problem. Our problem is, is that that's a never-ending process. I mean, I hope you can understand some of the concern when you get an opinion from the Court of Appeal and I practice in the state, I've been doing it for 26 years and there's an opinion that says in the beginning the complaint has got to be taken as true for purposes of demur. Here are the facts that have been pleaded. None of this stuff about conclusory pleading or anything like that that we have in the appellee's brief and one of the facts that's been pleaded is that it would be futile. And this is recited in the case. Yes, but you could have filed precisely that complaint before you filed this application. You could have made the same general allegation then gone ahead and proved, as you can now, that the development policy makes any development absolutely impossible. Well, you know, it may have been a little harder, but you could have done it. I believe, though, that this Court's opinion in the Egan's case prevents me from doing that. I think that what the Court said in Egan's is that I cannot come to court and state a 5th or 14th Amendment claim by virtue of land use regulations until I have first made an application to demonstrate how those regulations have been applied. We've done that. We've done that. And all we ask now is a day in court to prove exactly how they have been applied. One other point before it escapes me, and it's a point I would really like to make. I am, as far as the point when the taking occurs, we are, I'm very mindful of the position that you took in the opinion you wrote, Mr. Justice Stevens, in the Hamilton Bank case about the fact that the friction of the regulatory process is something to which all property owners hold their property. We don't disagree with that. But we want you to understand the California context. In California, we have something that's euphemistically referred to as a permit streamlining act, which allows one year to consider applications. The application procedure requires a substantial period of time before the application is deemed complete. So there is more than one year within which to consider and act on applications. We have a very, very tough issue exhaustion doctrine, which means that I cannot stand in front of a local planning body and fuzz over my arguments and then go to court and challenge them on something I didn't fully and fairly raise in front of them. So the local governing bodies that impose these restrictions, and these are very, you know, very restrictive things. They can be based entirely on aesthetics, entirely on how people feel about their community and where they live and so forth. they have a year plus some additional time to consider them and to consider all the issues and arguments that can be raised. And our position is that when they make a decision that's excessively burdensome, exceeds constitutional bounds, that they ought to be responsible for that and responsible in money damages. That to impose liability in such a case is just like what this court said in Maley v. Briggs very recently that it creates a necessary restraint, a valuable restraint. In order for us to reverse the Court of Appeals, we don't have to find that their interim damage is available for a taking. All we have to do is say that you've pleaded a taking. That's correct. And tell the court that the damages we prove, that we're entitled to be compensated, we're entitled to just compensation for the damages we prove. No, we don't have to say that. It doesn't seem to me. Your Court of Appeals has said, A, there's no taking, and B, if there were, there are no interim damages available. All you can do is get the taking set aside. We don't have to decide both those questions to adjudicate this case. We could simply decide you have alleged sufficient facts to show a taking. Well, we have asked you also to direct the court, the California courts, on what the remedy is. I'm mindful of the argument that's been made in the Solicitor General's brief, that that's an open question, that the question of whether compensation is required once you find a taking, as was stated in the San Diego dissent, or whether it's the compensation claim is just conditional, is still an open question here. So I suppose I have to agree with you, although we obviously are arguing, and I hope persuasively, that compensation is the only meaningful remedy. Mr. Eller, do you think ultimately it's possible that rightness is an element of a taking, that there can't be a taking until it's ripe for consideration by the courts? Yes, I really do. I mean, it's the same concept I was talking, that I was trying to explain in connection with our Permit Streamlining Act. We are prepared to accept the notion that until you make an application and go through the process and lay all your issues and arguments in front of the regulating, assuming that they have a process by which you can do that, which is very easy, by the way, if I hadn't run out of space, I had drafted an amendment, a proposed ordinance to include in my reply brief, and it was very short, that that should be required. We have no problem with that. We claim we did that, and we're prepared to prove it. We just need the chance. I would like to reserve the balance of my time for rebuttal, if I may. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. The appellant's complaint here alleges that the county denied one relatively intensive subdivision proposal based upon specific planning, public service, and safety reasons. we advance two basic propositions. First, denial of one specific subdivision proposal is not a final determination as to how the appellant's land may be used, and thus, no right-taking claim has been alleged by the complaint. Second, even if rightness is found to exist under these allegations, the allegations of this complaint do not stay to taking, whether analyzed under either the Just Compensation Clause or the Due Process Clause. I would like to address some of the remarks that were made in Council's prior argument in regard to the urban development policy of the county. Here we have a decision of the Court of Appeal that rules as a matter of California law that the denial of one specific map does not preclude other valuable uses under the county's judicially noticed zoning regulations. Oddly, the property owner wants to go to trial as a matter of proof to prove that the Court of Appeals was incorrect in interpreting the county's zoning regulations. Mr. I take it then you don't agree with footnote 3 in the petitioner's reply brief. No, we do not. It says about the Yolo County. No, we do not, Your Honor. Well, has it been your position in this case that the petitioner was entitled to some residential use of this land? Yes, as long as the property is zoned residential and planned residential in the county, which it is, the land use regulations of the county prescribe that that is a permitted use and there is no prohibition against that use. Has the county ever approved a use contrary to the city of Davis' recommendation or desire? I'm not sure, but they're right now embroiled in a fight over one and the outcome is unclear. It appears that, as a practical matter, the county has not and will not approve any such plan if the city of Davis doesn't say, fine, go ahead. Well, I don't know that that conclusion, I honestly couldn't reach that conclusion and I know the communities. the fact is that Yolo County is a very agricultural community and they have had a policy for many years that urban in quotes development occur within cities simply because cities are best able to provide the services that people demand when a urban type development occurs. That is a matter of public fiscal policy and planning policy that has been long in existence and... Well, but now, here the petitioner was asking for 160 houses on 44 acres. Would that be regarded as an urban development? I believe it would, Your Honor, and that's precisely the point with regard to this argument in footnote three. The term urban development is not defined at all. And in fact, if you... We didn't include these zoning classifications because this new argument has just been raised, but in the clerk's supplemental transcript, you'll find the county zoning ordinance, and if you look at the agricultural zone for general agriculture, or if you look at the residential suburban zone, which is a low-density residential zone, residences may be constructed up to one per half acre in residential suburban. And it's my position that you can't have a right-taking claim by fiat. Well, okay, so who was this zoned at the time of the application? The property was zoned R1, R2, R3, and R4. That's just precise areas. What does that mean? Well, each area, each geographic area, has a specific set of standards which outline the maximum densities that are permitted within that zone. Well, did this subdivision plant that was submitted with 159 lots? Did that comply with those existing zoning classification, or would it have required rezoning? No, the rezoning would not have been required. They were within the maximum densities permitted in those zoning classifications. But as is pointed out in the Pellant's opening brief, the fact that you have zoning on property only outlines the use and the maximum densities. The actual division for purposes of sale, lease, or financing, or for the development of public streets depends upon being within those maximums and also demonstrating that the plan and design will work under the applicable county policies, development policies. Why did the zoning board turn this down? The planning commission or the board of supervisors? The planning commission, the first instance. The planning commission, I do not recall whether they made formal findings or not. And I just yes, and those are exhibit C to the complaint and they're included in the joint appendix and they go into great detail. And in fact, on page 75, finding number 12 of the board specifically refers to this urban development type concept. and yet you can see if you read the board's evaluation that that was not a precluding factor. In other words, the board didn't say because of this policy we have to deny this project. They went through the entire list of public services that would be required to be provided to this subdivision and they determined that the application was inadequate because it made no provision as to how the services would be maintained and operated. Okay, well you've got some 18 reasons here for turning the thing down. And now supposing I'm in the petitioner's spot and I see these reasons, it says the city of Davis has officially opposed the subdivision because it is inconsistent with the general plan. Does that mean to me that until the city of Davis approves what I want to do, the board of supervisors of Yolo County is going to say no? Absolutely not. Well then why do they give this as a reason? Because the subdivision proposed the extension of a city street through city territory which the city would have had to have. But that's given as a separate reason under 6, the failure to extend Cowell Boulevard. That's right. So reason 10 just seems to be that if the city of Davis has officially opposed the subdivision, that is a reason for denying. No, you have to read 9, 10, and 11 together. They run in sequence. 9 says the board finds the tentative map does not provide for service. By any governmental entity. The agreement between the county and the city is that development in areas that are outside the city and outside the existing county service area must annex to one or the other. The next finding says the city of Davis has opposed because it's inconsistent with its general plan. And then 11 says therefore essentially the only means of providing sewer service is to annex to the CSA, the county service area, which the appellant has not done, has not taken any proceedings to do. That was not a finding that because of the city's opposition this proposal couldn't be approved. And that would clearly be contrary to California law. Cities do not have the ability to control land use outside their boundaries. They can plan and they can object like any other citizen could, but they cannot control that extraterritorial land use power. Again, it's our position that the attempt here to in effect prove, to claim that the appellant can prove that the uses which the Court of Appeal said are available to it is not a matter of proof. It's a matter of law based upon the regulations of the county, which under California law, the Court of Appeal has determined does permit the lesser residential or non-agricultural uses. Our rightness position essentially is that there were four routes to achieve a final determination from the county as to how the property might be utilized. The first of these was to submit a redesign that address the objections of the county to the first submittal. The Court in Penn Central recognized this, and the Court of Appeal here states specifically that the denial of that particular plan cannot be equated with a denial or with a refusal to permit any development.
